newsitem.title: USA: Spy Factory, owner plead guilty to smuggling.
newsitem.headline: Spy Factory, owner plead guilty to smuggling.

text.p: The Spy Factory, one of the nation's largest chains of "spy shops," its owner and two former executives pleaded guilty Monday to smuggling illegal bugging and wiretapping devices into the United States.

As part of the plea agreement, the defendants will forfeit the company's assets and its stores will be closed. The case had entered its second week of testimony in Manhattan federal court when the defendants agreed to plead guilty.

Ronald Kimball, owner of the San Antonio, Tex.-based chain, pleaded guilty to three counts of conspiracy to possess bugging and wire-tapping devices; using false statements to import these devices into the United States and smuggling the devices from Japan.
He faces a possible maximum prison term of 15 years and fines of $750,000.
Kimball also pleaded guilty on behalf of the corporation to charges that included money laundering.
At the time of the 1995 indictment, the Spy Factory had stores in Arizona, California, Colorado, Georgia, Illinois, Missouri, Nevada, Texas, Utah, Washington. The chain currently operates 11 stores.
An employee at one of the stores told an undercover Customs Service agent posing as a customer that most of the devices at that location were sold to local attorneys and private investigators.
Marlin Richardson, who had been general manager, and Tracy Ford, who had been deputy general manager at the time of the crimes also pleaded guilty.

Richardson admitted three counts related to the smuggling of illegal bugging and wire-tapping devices and faces a possible prison term of 15 years and fines of $750,000, and Ford pleaded guilty to two counts and faces a possible 10 year prison term and fines of $500,000.
U.S. District Judge Sonia Sotomayor set a June 12 sentencing date.
The defendants had originally been charged in an eight-count indictment in August 1995 accusing them of buying illegal devices from the Japanese firm Micro Electronics.
The items included bugging devices that were miniature transmitters hidden in everyday household and office items like pens, calculators and three-plug electric outlet adapters.

Spy Factory also sold so-called "wiretapping devices" that are miniature transmitters which attach directly to telephone lines and are capable of surreptitiously intercepting and transmitting both sides of a telephone conversation to a remote location.
